metadata.title: Only What The File Says.
metadata.subtitle: The Architecture Skill (ADR Decisions)
metadata.purpose: Take a Claude skill apart in the Teardown register: when Claude drafts or evaluates an architecture decision record, it isn't exercising design judgment — it's running the numbered steps its SKILL.md wrote down, in order. Name the trade-off: they optimized for repeatable, plan-before-act constraint logic at the expense of any judgment about which trade-off is right for your situation, and anything the file's steps don't cover.

beats.narration_text: Take a Claude skill apart, and here's what's inside. It's a folder — Claude reads it before it acts. This one's called architecture. Open it up: one file, SKILL.md. Plain language, no hidden logic underneath. Claude reads the file, then acts on what it says. The file is the program.

Here's how it runs. The pipeline lives in the Steps section. Claude opens it, reads each step in order, then executes it — top to bottom, linear, no branching, unless a step explicitly says otherwise. No hidden judgment layer picking which step to skip. What's on the page is what runs.

production_viz.label: READ THEN EXECUTE
production_viz.caption: linear, unless a step says otherwise

beats.narration_text: That's a design choice, and it costs something. They optimized for two things: repeatability, and making the constraint logic explicit before any recommendation lands — plan before act. Same inputs in, same reasoning out. Here's what it costs. This skill has exactly one job: create or evaluate an architecture decision record — choosing between technologies, documenting a trade-off, reviewing a design proposal, or designing a component from constraints. All of it lives inside that one file's script. Nothing outside it is covered. It won't tell you which trade-off is right for your situation — it formalizes the analysis; the call is still yours.

A skill runs the same steps every time you call it — never a step beyond what its file wrote down. They optimized for repeatable constraint logic; the judgment about which trade-off is right is still yours to make.

props.quote: A skill runs the same steps every time you call it — never a step beyond what its file wrote down. They optimized for repeatable constraint logic; the judgment about which trade-off is right is still yours to make.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: ask it to write a short SKILL.md for an architecture-decision skill, then run that skill on a real choice you're facing — say, PostgreSQL versus MongoDB for a specific workload. Watch it walk through the plan before it lands a recommendation, and watch the reasoning stay identical if you run the same inputs twice. Go deeper: hand it a case where the constraints genuinely don't decide the answer, and watch where the skill's steps stop and the model starts guessing.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how a Claude 'skill' runs an architecture decision. A Claude skill is a folder holding SKILL.md — a description telling Claude when to fire it, plus a numbered list of steps Claude reads and runs top to bottom, with no hidden judgment step. Write me a short SKILL.md for an architecture-decision skill: a description that triggers on 'choose between X and Y' / 'write an ADR' / 'evaluate this trade-off', plus four to six numbered steps that (1) restate the decision, (2) list constraints and non-negotiables, (3) enumerate the options, (4) score each option against each constraint, (5) name the trade-off being accepted, (6) walk me through the plan before recommending. Then run the skill on this decision: I'm building a small analytics service for a B2B SaaS. Peak load is 500 writes/second, mostly append-only event data with occasional joins for reporting. Team has three engineers, all more comfortable with SQL than document stores. Choose between PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Follow the steps in order and name the trade-off out loud. Do not skip the plan-before-recommend step.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: run the same decision through the skill twice — is the reasoning identical both times? Then hand it a case where the constraints genuinely don't pick a winner (say, two options tied on every axis you named), and watch where the skill's numbered steps end and the model starts filling in a preference. That's the line between what SKILL.md decides and what the model guesses.
